job.style: a step-by-step explanation of a process

passage: Vision is a fascinating process that begins when light reflects off objects and enters our eyes. Contrary to the idea that our eyes emit rays, we see only because light from an external source bounces off surfaces and reaches our retina. When light hits a rough surface like a wall, it undergoes diffused reflection, meaning it still reflects light, just in many directions. The first part of the eye that light encounters is the cornea, a transparent front surface that acts as a powerful lens to help focus incoming light. Behind this, the eye contains a flexible crystalline lens that changes its shape to adjust focus for objects at varying distances. The retina at the back of the eye is lined with specialized cells: rods, which are sensitive to dim light, and cones, which detect colors in bright light. Maintaining eye health requires a balanced diet rich in Vitamin A, found in carrots, leafy greens, and dairy, to support these cells. Finally, our brain processes images rapidly; because of the persistence of vision, we perceive a continuous stream of motion rather than individual gaps between images. This complex system ensures we can navigate our world effectively, provided we care for our eyes through proper nutrition and regular check-ups.

items.evidence: Contrary to the idea that our eyes emit rays, we see only because light from an external source bounces off surfaces and reaches our retina.
items.q: Why can't we see objects in a completely dark room?
options: No light is available to bounce off them
Our eyes cannot send out rays in darkness
Walls and objects stop reflecting at night
The cornea cannot focus anything in the dark
items.explain: We see only when light from a source bounces off objects into our eyes; eyes send out nothing.

wrong.why: thinks eyes send out rays that need light to work
thinks objects stop reflecting light in the dark
blames the eye's focusing part instead of missing light

items.evidence: When light hits a rough surface like a wall, it undergoes diffused reflection, meaning it still reflects light, just in many directions.
items.q: Why can you see a rough wall from every corner of a room?
options: It scatters light towards every side
It reflects no light, so our eyes find it
The laws of reflection stop working on it
It sends light only straight back to the source
items.explain: Diffused reflection means a rough wall still reflects light, but in many directions.

wrong.why: thinks rough surfaces do not reflect light at all
thinks reflection laws do not apply to rough surfaces
over-generalises smooth-mirror reflection to every surface

items.evidence: The first part of the eye that light encounters is the cornea, a transparent front surface that acts as a powerful lens to help focus incoming light.
items.q: Besides letting light in, what job does the cornea do in the eye?
options: It bends incoming light to help focus it
It only blocks dust and lets light pass
It changes shape for near and far objects
It senses colours when the light is bright
items.explain: The cornea is a transparent front lens that helps focus incoming light.

wrong.why: thinks the cornea only protects and does not focus
mixes up the cornea with the flexible lens behind it
mixes up the cornea with the colour-sensing cones

items.evidence: Behind this, the eye contains a flexible crystalline lens that changes its shape to adjust focus for objects at varying distances.
items.q: You look from a faraway tree to a book in your hand. What happens inside your eye?
options: The lens changes shape to refocus the light
The lens stays rigid and the focus stays fixed
The eye sends rays out to measure the distance
The cones turn into rods to adjust the focus
items.explain: The flexible lens changes shape to adjust focus for objects at different distances.

wrong.why: thinks the eye lens is rigid like glass
thinks the eye sends out rays to see
mixes up rods and cones with focusing

items.evidence: Finally, our brain processes images rapidly; because of the persistence of vision, we perceive a continuous stream of motion rather than individual gaps between images.
items.q: Why does a fast series of still film pictures look like smooth motion?
options: Our brain links them into unbroken movement
The eye is too slow to clear old images
Each picture is sent by the rods separately
Our eyes send rays that hold the pictures still
items.explain: Because of persistence of vision, we perceive continuous motion instead of gaps between images.

wrong.why: thinks persistence of vision is a slow-eye defect
mixes up rods with how images are joined
thinks eyes send out rays that hold the images
